**Luciano Pavarotti**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-1) (12 October 1935–6 September 2007) was an Italian operatic [tenor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenor "Tenor") who during the late part of his career crossed over into [popular music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_music "Popular music"), eventually becoming one of the most acclaimed tenors of all time. He made numerous recordings of complete [operas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opera "Opera") and individual [arias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aria "Aria"), gaining worldwide fame for his tone and the [nickname](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honorific_nicknames_in_popular_music "Honorific nicknames in popular music") "King of the [High Cs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_C "High C")".

As one of [the Three Tenors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Three_Tenors "The Three Tenors"), who performed their first concert during the [1990 FIFA World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990_FIFA_World_Cup "1990 FIFA World Cup") before a global audience, Pavarotti became well known for his televised concerts and media appearances. From the beginning of his professional career as a tenor in 1961 in Italy to his final performance of "[Nessun dorma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nessun_dorma "Nessun dorma")" at the [2006 Winter Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Winter_Olympics "2006 Winter Olympics") in [Turin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turin "Turin"), Pavarotti was at his best in [bel canto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel_canto "Bel canto") operas, pre-_[Aida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aida "Aida")_[Verdi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Verdi "Giuseppe Verdi") roles, and [Puccini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giacomo_Puccini "Giacomo Puccini") works such as _[La bohème](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La\_boh%C3%A8me "La bohème")_, _[Tosca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tosca "Tosca")_, _[Turandot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turandot "Turandot")_ and _[Madama Butterfly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madama\_Butterfly "Madama Butterfly")_. He sold more than 100 million records,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-2) and the [first Three Tenors recording](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carreras_Domingo_Pavarotti_in_Concert "Carreras Domingo Pavarotti in Concert") became the best-selling classical album of all time. Pavarotti was also noted for his charity work on behalf of [refugees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refugee "Refugee") and the [Red Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Red_Cross_and_Red_Crescent_Movement "International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement"), amongst others. He was appointed a [Knight Grand Cross of the Order of Merit of the Italian Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_Merit_of_the_Italian_Republic "Order of Merit of the Italian Republic") in 1988.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-3) Pavarotti died from [pancreatic cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pancreatic_cancer "Pancreatic cancer") on 6 September 2007.

## Biography

### Early life and musical training

Luciano Pavarotti was born on 12 October 1935 in a public housing block on the outskirts of [Modena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modena "Modena") in [Northern Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Italy "Northern Italy"), the son of Fernando Pavarotti, a baker and amateur tenor, and Adele Venturi, a cigar factory worker.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-tenor-4)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-5) Although he spoke fondly of his childhood, the family had little money; its four members were crowded into a two-room apartment. According to Pavarotti, his father had a fine tenor voice but rejected the possibility of a singing career because of nervousness. [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") forced the family out of the city in 1943. For the following year, they rented a single room from a farmer in the neighbouring countryside, where the young Pavarotti developed an interest in farming.

After abandoning the dream of becoming a [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football")[goalkeeper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goalkeeper_(association_football) "Goalkeeper (association football)"), Pavarotti spent seven years in vocal training. Pavarotti's earliest musical influences were his father's records, most of them featuring the popular tenors of the day—[Beniamino Gigli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beniamino_Gigli "Beniamino Gigli"), [Giovanni Martinelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giovanni_Martinelli "Giovanni Martinelli"), [Tito Schipa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tito_Schipa "Tito Schipa"), and [Enrico Caruso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enrico_Caruso "Enrico Caruso").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-tenor-4) Pavarotti's favourite tenor and idol was [Giuseppe Di Stefano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Di_Stefano "Giuseppe Di Stefano").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-tenor-4) He was also deeply influenced by [Mario Lanza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario_Lanza "Mario Lanza"), saying: "In my teens I used to go to Mario Lanza movies and then come home and imitate him in the mirror". At around the age of nine, he began singing with his father in a small local church choir.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-tenor-4)

In addition to music, as a child, Pavarotti enjoyed playing [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football"). When he graduated from the Scuola Magistrale, he was interested in pursuing a career as a professional football [goalkeeper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goalkeeper_(association_football) "Goalkeeper (association football)"), but his mother convinced him to train as a teacher. He subsequently taught in an elementary school for two years but finally decided to pursue a music career. His father, recognising the risk involved, only reluctantly gave his consent. Pavarotti began the serious study of music in 1954 at the age of 19 with [Arrigo Pola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrigo_Pola "Arrigo Pola"), a respected teacher and professional tenor in Modena who offered to teach him without remuneration. According to conductor [Richard Bonynge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bonynge "Richard Bonynge"), Pavarotti never learned to read music.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-6)

In 1955, he experienced his first singing success when he was a member of the Corale Rossini, a [male voice choir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Male_voice_choir "Male voice choir") from Modena that also included his father, which won first prize at the [International Eisteddfod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llangollen_International_Musical_Eisteddfod "Llangollen International Musical Eisteddfod") in [Llangollen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llangollen "Llangollen"), Wales. He later said that this was the most important experience of his life, and that it inspired him to become a professional singer.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-7)

When his teacher, [Arrigo Pola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrigo_Pola "Arrigo Pola"), moved to Japan, Pavarotti became a student of [Ettore Campogalliani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ettore_Campogalliani "Ettore Campogalliani"), who at that time was also teaching Pavarotti's childhood friend, [Mirella Freni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirella_Freni "Mirella Freni"), whose mother worked with Luciano's mother in the cigar factory. Like Pavarotti, Freni went on to become a successful opera singer; they collaborated in various stage performances and recordings together.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-tenor-4)

During his years of musical study, Pavarotti held part-time jobs to sustain himself—first as an elementary school teacher and then as an insurance salesman. The first six years of study resulted in only a few recitals, all in small towns and without pay. When a [nodule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vocal_fold_nodule "Vocal fold nodule") developed on his [vocal cords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vocal_folds "Vocal folds"), causing a _"disastrous"_ concert in [Ferrara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferrara "Ferrara"), he decided to give up singing. Pavarotti attributed his immediate improvement to the psychological release connected with this decision. Whatever the reason, the nodule not only disappeared but, as he related in his autobiography: "Everything I had learned came together with my natural voice to make the sound I had been struggling so hard to achieve".

### Career: 1960s–1970s

Pavarotti began his career as a tenor in smaller regional Italian opera houses. After winning the Achille Peri International Competition, he made his debut as Rodolfo in _[La bohème](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La\_boh%C3%A8me "La bohème")_ at the [Teatro Municipale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teatro_Municipale_di_Reggio "Teatro Municipale di Reggio") in [Reggio Emilia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reggio_Emilia "Reggio Emilia") in April 1961, conducted by [Francesco Molinari-Pradelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_Molinari-Pradelli "Francesco Molinari-Pradelli") and staged by [Mafalda Favero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mafalda_Favero "Mafalda Favero").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-tenor-4) His first known recording of "[Che gelida manina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Che_gelida_manina "Che gelida manina")" was recorded during this performance.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-8)

In December 1961, Pavarotti made his first international appearance in _[La traviata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La\_traviata "La traviata")_ in [Belgrade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgrade "Belgrade"), [Yugoslavia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Federal_Republic_of_Yugoslavia "Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-9)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-10) On 23 February 1963, he debuted at the [Vienna State Opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna_State_Opera "Vienna State Opera") in the same role. In March and April 1963, Pavarotti performed again in Vienna as Rodolfo and as Duca di Mantova in _[Rigoletto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rigoletto "Rigoletto")_. The same year, he performed his first solo non-opera concert outside Italy when he sang in [Dundalk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dundalk "Dundalk"), Ireland, for the St Cecilia's Gramophone Society.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-dundalk-11) He was engaged by the Dublin Grand Opera Society to sing The Duke of Mantua in Verdi's [Rigoletto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rigoletto "Rigoletto") in May and June,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-dundalk-11) and his [Royal Opera House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Royal_Opera "The Royal Opera") debut, where he replaced an indisposed [Giuseppe Di Stefano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Di_Stefano "Giuseppe Di Stefano") as Rodolfo.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-aboutvoice-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-13) In September 1963, he made his debut at Covent Garden in La Boheme, which gave his career a boost.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-14)

In 1964, Pavarotti appeared as Idamante in _[Idomeneo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idomeneo "Idomeneo")_ at [Glyndebourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glyndebourne_Festival_Opera "Glyndebourne Festival Opera")[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-15) and was engaged by the Dublin Grand Opera Society to sing Rodolfo in [Giacomo Puccini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giacomo_Puccini "Giacomo Puccini")'s _[La bohème](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La\_boh%C3%A8me "La bohème")_ and Alfredo in Giuseppe Verdi's _[La Traviata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La\_Traviata "La Traviata")_. Reviewers favourably comment on his singing.

Pavarotti sang with Joan Sutherland when he made his American début with the [Greater Miami Opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida_Grand_Opera "Florida Grand Opera") in February 1965, singing in [Gaetano Donizetti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaetano_Donizetti "Gaetano Donizetti")'s _[Lucia di Lammermoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucia\_di\_Lammermoor "Lucia di Lammermoor")_ on the stage of the [Miami-Dade County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami-Dade_County "Miami-Dade County") Auditorium in Miami. The tenor that was scheduled to perform that night became ill with no understudy. Sutherland recommended Pavarotti as he was acquainted with the role. On 28 April, Pavarotti made his [La Scala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Scala "La Scala") debut in the revival of the [Franco Zeffirelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franco_Zeffirelli "Franco Zeffirelli") production of _La bohème_, with his childhood friend [Mirella Freni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirella_Freni "Mirella Freni") singing Mimi and [Herbert von Karajan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_von_Karajan "Herbert von Karajan") conducting. Karajan had requested the singer's engagement.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-tenor-4)

[Joan Sutherland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_Sutherland "Joan Sutherland") and her conductor husband, [Richard Bonynge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bonynge "Richard Bonynge") sought a tall tenor to take along on their 1965 tour to Australia.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-tenor-4)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-aboutvoice-12) During the Australia tour in summer 1965, Sutherland and Pavarotti sang forty performances over two months. Pavarotti later credited Sutherland for the breathing and diaphragm technique that sustained him through his career.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-tenor-4)

After the extended Australian tour, he returned to La Scala, where he added Tebaldo from _[I Capuleti e i Montecchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I\_Capuleti\_e\_i\_Montecchi "I Capuleti e i Montecchi")_ to his repertoire on 26 March 1966, with [Giacomo Aragall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giacomo_Aragall "Giacomo Aragall") as Romeo.

His first appearance as Tonio in Donizetti's _[La fille du régiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La\_fille\_du\_r%C3%A9giment "La fille du régiment")_ took place at the Royal Opera House, Covent Garden, on 2 June 1966. In this performance, he was the first tenor to deliver nine natural high Cs in the aria "Ah! mes amis".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-tenor-4)

He scored another major triumph in Rome on 20 November 1969 when he sang in _[I Lombardi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I\_Lombardi\_alla\_prima\_crociata "I Lombardi alla prima crociata")_ opposite [Renata Scotto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renata_Scotto "Renata Scotto"). This was recorded on a private label and widely distributed, as were various recordings of his _I Capuleti e i Montecchi_, usually with Aragall. Early commercial recordings included a recital of Donizetti (the aria from _[Don Sebastiano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dom\_S%C3%A9bastien "Dom Sébastien")_ were particularly highly regarded) and [Verdi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Verdi "Giuseppe Verdi")[arias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aria "Aria"), as well as a complete _[L'elisir d'amore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L'elisir\_d'amore "L'elisir d'amore")_ with Sutherland.

His breakthrough in the United States came on 17 February 1972, in a production of _La fille du régiment_ at New York's [Metropolitan Opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Opera "Metropolitan Opera"), in which he hit nine [high Cs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenor_C "Tenor C") in the signature [aria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aria "Aria") and had seventeen curtain calls.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-16) This earned him the nickname "King of the High Cs".[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-17)

Pavarotti sang his international [recital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concert#Recital "Concert") début at [William Jewell College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Jewell_College "William Jewell College") in [Liberty, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberty,_Missouri "Liberty, Missouri"), on 1 February 1973, as part of the college's Fine Arts Program, now known as the Harriman–Jewell Series.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-:0-18) According to his manager at the time, Pavarotti clutched a handkerchief throughout this recital because he had a lingering cold.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-19) Pavarotti himself explained that he needed the handkerchief, since he didn't know what to do with his hands.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-:0-18) The prop became a signature part of his solo performances.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-20) He began to give frequent television performances, starting with his performances as Rodolfo (_La bohème_) in the first [Live from the Met](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_from_the_Met "Live from the Met") telecast in March 1977, which attracted one of the largest audiences ever for a televised opera.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-21) He won [Grammy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award "Grammy Award") awards and [platinum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platinum_disc "Platinum disc") and [gold discs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_disc "Gold disc") for his performances.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In 1976, Pavarotti debuted at the [Salzburg Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salzburg_Festival "Salzburg Festival"), appearing in a solo recital on 31 July, accompanied by pianist Leone Magiera. Pavarotti returned to the festival in 1978 with a recital and as the Italian singer in _[Der Rosenkavalier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Der\_Rosenkavalier "Der Rosenkavalier")_ in 1983 with _[Idomeneo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idomeneo "Idomeneo")_, and both in 1985 and 1988 with solo recitals. In 1979, he was profiled in a cover story in the weekly magazine _[Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time\_(magazine) "Time (magazine)")_.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-22) That same year saw Pavarotti's return to the [Vienna State Opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna_State_Opera "Vienna State Opera") after an absence of fourteen years. With Herbert von Karajan conducting, Pavarotti sang Manrico in _[Il trovatore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Il\_trovatore "Il trovatore")_. In 1978, he appeared in a solo recital on _[Live from Lincoln Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live\_from\_Lincoln\_Center "Live from Lincoln Center")_.

### Career: 1980s–1990s

At the beginning of the 1980s, he set up The Pavarotti International Voice Competition for young singers, performing with the winners in 1982 in excerpts of _La bohème_ and _L'elisir d'amore_. The second competition, in 1986, staged excerpts of _La bohème_ and _Un ballo in maschera_. To celebrate the 25th anniversary of his career, he brought the winners of the competition to Italy for gala performances of _La bohème_ in Modena and [Genoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genoa "Genoa"), and then to China, where they staged performances of _La bohème_ in Beijing ([Peking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peking "Peking")). To conclude the visit, Pavarotti performed the inaugural concert in the [Great Hall of the People](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Hall_of_the_People "Great Hall of the People") before 10,000 people, receiving a [standing ovation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standing_ovation "Standing ovation") for nine high Cs.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-23)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-24) The third competition in 1989 again staged performances of _L'elisir d'amore_ and _Un ballo in maschera_. The winners of the fifth competition accompanied Pavarotti in performances in [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia") in 1997.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In the mid-1980s, Pavarotti returned to two opera houses that had provided him with important breakthroughs, the [Vienna State Opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna_State_Opera "Vienna State Opera") and [La Scala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Scala "La Scala"). Vienna saw Pavarotti as Rodolfo in _La bohème_ with [Carlos Kleiber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Kleiber "Carlos Kleiber") conducting, and again Mirella Freni was Mimi; as Nemorino in _L'elisir d'amore_; as Radames in _Aida_ conducted by Lorin Maazel; as Rodolfo in _Luisa Miller_; and as Gustavo in _Un ballo in maschera_ conducted by Claudio Abbado. In 1996, Pavarotti appeared for the last time at the Staatsoper in _Andrea Chénier_. Throughout the 1980s and 90s, promoters [Tibor Rudas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibor_Rudas "Tibor Rudas") and [Harvey Goldsmith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_Goldsmith "Harvey Goldsmith") booked Pavarotti into increasingly larger venues.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/21/Vincenzo_Mollica%2C_Pavarotti%2C_Lucio_Dalla_e_Zucchero_al_Pavarotti_e_friends_1992.jpg/250px-Vincenzo_Mollica%2C_Pavarotti%2C_Lucio_Dalla_e_Zucchero_al_Pavarotti_e_friends_1992.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Vincenzo_Mollica,_Pavarotti,_Lucio_Dalla_e_Zucchero_al_Pavarotti_e_friends_1992.jpg)

From left: journalist Vincenzo Mollica, Pavarotti, [Lucio Dalla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucio_Dalla "Lucio Dalla") and [Zucchero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zucchero_Fornaciari "Zucchero Fornaciari") on the first edition of _[Pavarotti & Friends](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pavarotti\_&\_Friends "Pavarotti & Friends")_ (1992)

In 1985, Pavarotti sang Radames at La Scala opposite Maria Chiara in a Luca Ronconi production conducted by Maazel, recorded on video. His performance of the aria "Celeste Aida" received a two-minute ovation on the opening night.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] He was reunited with Mirella Freni for the San Francisco Opera production of _La bohème_ in 1988, also recorded on video. In 1992, La Scala saw Pavarotti in a new Zeffirelli production of _Don Carlos_, conducted by Riccardo Muti.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-25)

Pavarotti became even better known throughout the world in 1990 when his rendition of the aria "[Nessun dorma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nessun_dorma "Nessun dorma")" from [Giacomo Puccini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giacomo_Puccini "Giacomo Puccini")'s _[Turandot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turandot "Turandot")_ was taken as the theme song of [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC")'s coverage of the [1990 FIFA World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990_FIFA_World_Cup "1990 FIFA World Cup") in Italy. The aria achieved pop status, became the World Cup soundtrack, and remained his trademark song.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-26) This was followed by the first [Three Tenors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Tenors "Three Tenors") concert, held on the eve of the [1990 FIFA World Cup Final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990_FIFA_World_Cup_Final "1990 FIFA World Cup Final") at the ancient [Baths of Caracalla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baths_of_Caracalla "Baths of Caracalla") in Rome with fellow tenors [Plácido Domingo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pl%C3%A1cido_Domingo "Plácido Domingo") and [José Carreras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Carreras "José Carreras") and conductor [Zubin Mehta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zubin_Mehta "Zubin Mehta"). The performance for the World Cup closing concert captivated a global audience, and it became the biggest-selling classical record of all time.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-27) A highlight of the concert, in which Pavarotti sang the opening verses using extended vocal runs for di Capua's "['O sole mio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/'O_sole_mio "'O sole mio")" and which was in turn perfectly repeated note-for-note by Domingo and Carreras. The recorded album sold millions of copies,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-28) and the [first Three Tenors recording](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carreras_Domingo_Pavarotti_in_Concert "Carreras Domingo Pavarotti in Concert") became the best-selling classical album of all time.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-29) Throughout the 1990s, Pavarotti appeared in outdoor concerts, [including his televised concert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pavarotti_in_the_Park "Pavarotti in the Park") in London's [Hyde Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyde_Park,_London "Hyde Park, London"), which drew a record attendance of 150,000. In June 1993, more than 500,000 listeners gathered for his free performance on the Great Lawn of New York's [Central Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Park "Central Park"), while millions more around the world watched on television.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-30) The following September, in the shadow of the [Eiffel Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eiffel_Tower "Eiffel Tower") in Paris, he sang for an estimated crowd of 300,000.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-31) Following on from the original 1990 concert, the Three Tenors concerts were held during the three subsequent [FIFA World Cup Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_FIFA_World_Cup_finals "List of FIFA World Cup finals"), in 1994 in Los Angeles, 1998 in Paris, and 2002 in Yokohama.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-FIFA-32)

[Elton John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elton_John "Elton John") and Pavarotti in Modena, 1996

In September 1995, Pavarotti performed Schubert's [Ave Maria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ave_Maria_(Schubert) "Ave Maria (Schubert)") along with [Dolores O'Riordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolores_O'Riordan "Dolores O'Riordan"); [Diana, Princess of Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diana,_Princess_of_Wales "Diana, Princess of Wales"), who attended the live performance, told O'Riordan that the song brought her to tears.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-33)

In 1995, Pavarotti's friends, [Lara Saint Paul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lara_Saint_Paul "Lara Saint Paul") (as Lara Cariaggi) and her husband showman Pier Quinto Cariaggi, who had produced and organised Pavarotti's 1990 FIFA World Cup Celebration Concert at the [PalaTrussardi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PalaSharp "PalaSharp") in Milan, produced and wrote the television documentary _The Best is Yet to Come_, an extensive biography about the life of Pavarotti. Lara Saint Paul was the interviewer for the documentary with Pavarotti, who spoke candidly about his life and career.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-34)

Pavarotti earned a reputation as "The King of Cancellations" by frequently backing out of performances, and his unreliable nature led to poor relationships with some opera houses.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-35) This was brought into focus in 1989 when [Ardis Krainik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ardis_Krainik "Ardis Krainik") of the [Lyric Opera of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyric_Opera_of_Chicago "Lyric Opera of Chicago") severed the house's 15-year relationship with the tenor.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-Ref-1-36) Over an eight-year period, Pavarotti had cancelled 26 out of 41 scheduled appearances at the Lyric, and the decisive move by Krainik to ban him for life was well noted throughout the opera world,[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-37) after the performer walked away from a season premiere less than two weeks before rehearsals began, saying pain from a sciatic nerve required two months of treatment.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-38) On 12 December 1998, he became the first (and, to date, only) opera singer to perform on _[Saturday Night Live](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturday\_Night\_Live "Saturday Night Live")_, singing alongside [Vanessa L. Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanessa_L._Williams "Vanessa L. Williams"). He also sang with [U2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U2 "U2") in the band's 1995 song "[Miss Sarajevo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miss_Sarajevo "Miss Sarajevo")" and with [Mercedes Sosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercedes_Sosa "Mercedes Sosa") in a big concert at the [Boca Juniors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boca_Juniors "Boca Juniors") arena [La Bombonera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Alberto_J._Armando "Estadio Alberto J. Armando") in Buenos Aires, Argentina, in 1999. In 1998, Pavarotti was presented with the [Grammy Legend Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Legend_Award "Grammy Legend Award").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-39)

### Career: Early 2000s

[![Image 11](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f7/Luciano_Pavarotti_15.06.02_cropped.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Luciano_Pavarotti_15.06.02_cropped.jpg)

Luciano Pavarotti performing on 15 June 2002 at a concert in the [Stade Vélodrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stade_V%C3%A9lodrome "Stade Vélodrome") in [Marseille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marseille "Marseille")

In September 2003, he released his final compilation—and his first and only "crossover" album, _Ti Adoro._ Most of the 13 songs were written and produced by Michele Centonze, who had already helped produce the "Pavarotti & Friends" concerts between 1998 and 2000.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-40) The tenor described the album as a wedding gift to Nicoletta Mantovani.

In 2004, one of Pavarotti's former managers, [Herbert Breslin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Breslin "Herbert Breslin"), published a book, _The King&I_.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-Ref-1-36) Seen by critics as bitter and sensationalistic[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_], it is critical of the singer's acting (in opera), his inability to read music well and learn parts, and his personal conduct, although acknowledging their success together. In an interview in 2005 with [Jeremy Paxman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Paxman "Jeremy Paxman") on the [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC"), Pavarotti rejected the allegation that he could not read music, although he acknowledged he did not read orchestral scores.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-41)

His awards and honours include [Kennedy Center Honors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Center_Honors "Kennedy Center Honors") in 2001. He also holds two [Guinness World Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guinness_World_Records "Guinness World Records"): one for receiving the most [curtain calls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curtain_call "Curtain call") (165)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-42) and another for the best-selling [classical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_music_era "Classical music era") album (_[Carreras Domingo Pavarotti in Concert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carreras\_Domingo\_Pavarotti\_in\_Concert "Carreras Domingo Pavarotti in Concert")_ by [the Three Tenors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Three_Tenors "The Three Tenors"); the latter record is thus shared by fellow tenors [Plácido Domingo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pl%C3%A1cido_Domingo "Plácido Domingo") and [José Carreras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Carreras "José Carreras")).[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-43)

### Final performances

On 13 March 2004, Pavarotti gave his last performance in an opera at the [New York Metropolitan Opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Metropolitan_Opera "New York Metropolitan Opera"), for which he received a long standing ovation for his role as the painter Mario Cavaradossi in [Giacomo Puccini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giacomo_Puccini "Giacomo Puccini")'s _[Tosca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tosca "Tosca")_.

On 1 December 2004, he announced a 40-city [farewell tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farewell_tour "Farewell tour"), produced by [Harvey Goldsmith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_Goldsmith "Harvey Goldsmith"). His last full-scale performance was in Taiwan in December 2005.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-44)

Pavarotti performing a lip-synced version of "[Nessun dorma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nessun_dorma "Nessun dorma")" at the [2006 Winter Olympics opening ceremony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Winter_Olympics_opening_ceremony "2006 Winter Olympics opening ceremony")

On 10 February 2006, Pavarotti performed "[Nessun dorma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nessun_dorma "Nessun dorma")" as the last act of the [2006 Winter Olympics opening ceremony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Winter_Olympics_opening_ceremony "2006 Winter Olympics opening ceremony") in [Turin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turin "Turin"), Italy, his final performance. However, as he was unsure of the strength of his voice due to health issues, he prerecorded the song and [lip synced](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lip_sync "Lip sync") the performance, with approval from the [International Olympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Olympic_Committee "International Olympic Committee").[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-mimed-45) His performance received the longest and loudest ovation of the night.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-46)

## Personal life

### Relationships

In the 1950s, Pavarotti met Adua Veroni. They married in 1961 and had three daughters: Lorenza, Cristina, and Giuliana. They separated in the early 1990s and divorced in 2002.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-nytobit-47)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-48)

On 13 December 2003, he married his second wife and former personal assistant, Nicoletta Mantovani (born 1969, 34 years younger than Pavarotti), with whom he already had another daughter, Alice (born in January 2003), when Pavarotti was 67. Her twin brother, Riccardo, was [stillborn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stillborn "Stillborn").[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-49)

### Tax evasion charges

Pavarotti long claimed [Monte Carlo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Carlo "Monte Carlo") in the [tax haven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax_haven "Tax haven") of [Monaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monaco "Monaco") as his [tax residence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax_residence "Tax residence"), but, in 1999, an Italian court rejected that claim by ruling that his Monaco address could not accommodate his entire family and accused him of [tax evasion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax_evasion "Tax evasion"). In 2000, Pavarotti agreed to pay the Italian government 24 million [Italian lire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_lira "Italian lira"), and in 2001, he was acquitted in an Italian court of tax evasion charges.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-50)

### Health issues and death

Pavarotti had long struggled with his weight and was 350 pounds (160 kg) at his heaviest. In 1998, he had double hip replacement surgery and knee surgery.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-51)

In March 2005, Pavarotti underwent neck surgery to repair two [vertebrae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertebrae "Vertebrae"). In early 2006, he underwent back surgery and contracted an infection while in the hospital in New York, forcing cancellation of concerts in the US, Canada, and the UK.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-52)

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/Grave_of_Luciano_Pavarotti_and_his_family.jpg/250px-Grave_of_Luciano_Pavarotti_and_his_family.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Grave_of_Luciano_Pavarotti_and_his_family.jpg)

Grave of Luciano Pavarotti and his family in [Montale Rangone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montale_Rangone "Montale Rangone")[[it](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montale%20Rangone "it:Montale Rangone")]

In July 2006, after suffering from abdominal discomfort and weight loss, Pavarotti was diagnosed with [pancreatic cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pancreatic_cancer "Pancreatic cancer"), which has a very low survival rate. He cancelled the remainder of his concerts and underwent successful surgery at [Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial_Sloan_Kettering_Cancer_Center "Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center") to remove the tumour. However, the cancer had already undergone [metastasis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metastasis "Metastasis").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-53) Pavarotti died at his home in Modena on 6 September 2007. His manager noted that "he remained positive until finally succumbing to the last stages of his illness".[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-54)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-55)

Pavarotti's funeral was held at [Modena Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modena_Cathedral "Modena Cathedral"). Prime Minister [Romano Prodi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romano_Prodi "Romano Prodi") and [Kofi Annan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kofi_Annan "Kofi Annan") attended.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-56) The [Frecce Tricolori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frecce_Tricolori "Frecce Tricolori"), the aerobatic demonstration team of the [Italian Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Air_Force "Italian Air Force"), flew overhead, leaving green-white-red smoke trails. After a funeral procession through the centre of Modena, Pavarotti's coffin was taken the final ten kilometres (6 miles) to Montale Rangone, a village part of [Castelnuovo Rangone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castelnuovo_Rangone "Castelnuovo Rangone"), and was interred in the Pavarotti family crypt. The funeral, in its entirety, was also telecast live on [CNN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNN "CNN"). The [Vienna State Opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna_State_Opera "Vienna State Opera") and the [Salzburg Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salzburg_Festival "Salzburg Festival") hall flew black flags in mourning.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-loss-57) Tributes were published by many opera houses, such as London's [Royal Opera House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Opera_House "Royal Opera House").[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-loss-57)

At the time of his death in September 2007, he was survived by his wife, his four daughters, and one granddaughter.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-nytobit-47)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-58)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-59)

#### Estate

Pavarotti's estate was valued at as much as €300 million before deducting debts and mortgages of €18 million. It included a villa in Pesaro, a home in Modena (now a museum), a high-profile co-op apartment in New York City, an apartment in Monte Carlo, international royalties, stage costumes, and art collections.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-60)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-deal-61)

Pavarotti had three wills: one, under Italian law, for his Italian assets, one, under US law, for his US assets, and a third handwritten will that reduced his wife's share.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-62)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-63)

His Italian will gave half of his estate to his second wife, Nicoletta Mantovani, and half to his four daughters, split equally amongst them; the second will gave all his U.S. holdings to Mantovani. Pavarotti's daughters felt shortchanged and contested the will, and a [Pesaro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pesaro "Pesaro")[public prosecutor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_prosecutor "Public prosecutor"), Massimo di Patria, investigated allegations that Pavarotti was not of [sound mind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound_mind "Sound mind") when he signed the will. As part of a compromise confirmed by a judge in July 2008, the daughters were given the house in Pesaro.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-deal-61)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-64)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-65)

### Humanitarianism

Pavarotti annually hosted the Pavarotti & Friends charity concerts in his home town of [Modena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modena "Modena")[Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy"), joining with singers from all parts of the music industry, including [B.B. King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B.B._King "B.B. King"), [Andrea Bocelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrea_Bocelli "Andrea Bocelli"), [Zucchero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zucchero "Zucchero"), [Jon Bon Jovi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Bon_Jovi "Jon Bon Jovi"), [Bryan Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryan_Adams "Bryan Adams"), [Bono](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bono "Bono"), [James Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Brown "James Brown"), [Mariah Carey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariah_Carey "Mariah Carey"), [Eric Clapton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Clapton "Eric Clapton"), [Dolores O'Riordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolores_O'Riordan "Dolores O'Riordan"), [Sheryl Crow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheryl_Crow "Sheryl Crow"), [Céline Dion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%A9line_Dion "Céline Dion"), [Anastacia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anastacia "Anastacia"), [Elton John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elton_John "Elton John"), [Deep Purple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_Purple "Deep Purple"), [Meat Loaf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meat_Loaf "Meat Loaf"), [Queen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_(band) "Queen (band)"), [George Michael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Michael "George Michael"), [Tracy Chapman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tracy_Chapman "Tracy Chapman"), the [Spice Girls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spice_Girls "Spice Girls"), [Sting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sting_(musician) "Sting (musician)") and [Barry White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barry_White "Barry White") to raise money for several UN causes. Pavarotti was a close friend of [Diana, Princess of Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diana,_Princess_of_Wales "Diana, Princess of Wales"). They raised money for the elimination of [land mines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_mines "Land mines") worldwide.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-70)

In 1998, he was appointed the [United Nations Messenger of Peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Messenger_of_Peace "United Nations Messenger of Peace"), using his fame to raise awareness of UN issues, including the [Millennium Development Goals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millennium_Development_Goals "Millennium Development Goals"), [HIV/AIDS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HIV/AIDS "HIV/AIDS"), [child rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_rights "Child rights"), [urban slums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slums "Slums") and poverty.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-71)

In June 1999, Pavarotti performed a charity benefit concert at [Camille Chamoun Sports City Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camille_Chamoun_Sports_City_Stadium "Camille Chamoun Sports City Stadium") in [Beirut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beirut "Beirut"). The largest concert held in Beirut since the end of the [Lebanese Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebanese_Civil_War "Lebanese Civil War"), it was attended by 20,000 people from all over the [Persian Gulf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_Gulf "Persian Gulf").[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-72)

In 1999, he also hosted a charity benefit concert to build a school in Guatemala, for Guatemalan civil war orphans. It was named after him [Centro Educativo Pavarotti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centro_Educativo_Pavarotti "Centro Educativo Pavarotti"). Now the foundation of Nobel Prize winner Rigoberta Menchú Tum is running the school.

#### Humanitarian honours

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/ff/Handprint_of_Luciano_Pavarotti.jpg/250px-Handprint_of_Luciano_Pavarotti.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Handprint_of_Luciano_Pavarotti.jpg)

Handprint of Luciano Pavarotti. Atlantic City Boardwalk, New Jersey USA 2006.

In 2001, Pavarotti received the [Nansen Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nansen_Medal "Nansen Medal") from the [UN High Commission for Refugees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UN_High_Commission_for_Refugees "UN High Commission for Refugees") for his efforts in raising money on behalf of [refugees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refugee "Refugee") worldwide. Through benefit concerts and volunteer work, he has raised more than any other individual.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-73)

Also in 2001, Pavarotti was chosen one of that year's five recipients by the President and First Lady as an honoree for their lifetime achievements in the arts at the [White House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House "White House"), followed by the [Kennedy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Center "Kennedy Center"); the [Kennedy Center Honors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Center_Honors "Kennedy Center Honors"), He was surprised by the appearance of [Secretary-General of the United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary-General_of_the_United_Nations "Secretary-General of the United Nations") and that year's winner of the [Nobel Peace Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Peace_Prize "Nobel Peace Prize"), [Kofi Annan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kofi_Annan "Kofi Annan"), who lauded him for his contribution to humankind. Six months prior, Pavarotti had held a large charity concert for Afghan refugees, particularly children in his home town of Modena, Italy.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-Kennedy_Center_Honors1-74)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-75)

Other honours he received include the _"Freedom of London Award"_ and The [Red Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Cross "Red Cross")_"Award for Services to Humanity"_, for his work in raising money for that organisation, and the 1998 _"[MusiCares Person of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MusiCares\_Person\_of\_the\_Year "MusiCares Person of the Year")"_, given to humanitarian heroes by the [National Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Academy_of_Recording_Arts_and_Sciences "National Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences").[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-76)

**Luciano Pavarotti**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-1) (12 October 1935–6 September 2007) was an Italian operatic [tenor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenor "Tenor") who during the late part of his career crossed over into [popular music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_music "Popular music"), eventually becoming one of the most acclaimed tenors of all time. He made numerous recordings of complete [operas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opera "Opera") and individual [arias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aria "Aria"), gaining worldwide fame for his tone and the [nickname](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honorific_nicknames_in_popular_music "Honorific nicknames in popular music") "King of the [High Cs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_C "High C")".

As one of [the Three Tenors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Three_Tenors "The Three Tenors"), who performed their first concert during the [1990 FIFA World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990_FIFA_World_Cup "1990 FIFA World Cup") before a global audience, Pavarotti became well known for his televised concerts and media appearances. From the beginning of his professional career as a tenor in 1961 in Italy to his final performance of "[Nessun dorma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nessun_dorma "Nessun dorma")" at the [2006 Winter Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Winter_Olympics "2006 Winter Olympics") in [Turin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turin "Turin"), Pavarotti was at his best in [bel canto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel_canto "Bel canto") operas, pre-_[Aida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aida "Aida")_[Verdi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Verdi "Giuseppe Verdi") roles, and [Puccini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giacomo_Puccini "Giacomo Puccini") works such as _[La bohème](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La\_boh%C3%A8me "La bohème")_, _[Tosca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tosca "Tosca")_, _[Turandot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turandot "Turandot")_ and _[Madama Butterfly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madama\_Butterfly "Madama Butterfly")_. He sold more than 100 million records,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-2) and the [first Three Tenors recording](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carreras_Domingo_Pavarotti_in_Concert "Carreras Domingo Pavarotti in Concert") became the best-selling classical album of all time. Pavarotti was also noted for his charity work on behalf of [refugees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refugee "Refugee") and the [Red Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Red_Cross_and_Red_Crescent_Movement "International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement"), amongst others. He was appointed a [Knight Grand Cross of the Order of Merit of the Italian Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_Merit_of_the_Italian_Republic "Order of Merit of the Italian Republic") in 1988.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-3) Pavarotti died from [pancreatic cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pancreatic_cancer "Pancreatic cancer") on 6 September 2007.

## Biography

### Early life and musical training

Luciano Pavarotti was born on 12 October 1935 in a public housing block on the outskirts of [Modena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modena "Modena") in [Northern Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Italy "Northern Italy"), the son of Fernando Pavarotti, a baker and amateur tenor, and Adele Venturi, a cigar factory worker.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-tenor-4)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-5) Although he spoke fondly of his childhood, the family had little money; its four members were crowded into a two-room apartment. According to Pavarotti, his father had a fine tenor voice but rejected the possibility of a singing career because of nervousness. [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") forced the family out of the city in 1943. For the following year, they rented a single room from a farmer in the neighbouring countryside, where the young Pavarotti developed an interest in farming.

After abandoning the dream of becoming a [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football")[goalkeeper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goalkeeper_(association_football) "Goalkeeper (association football)"), Pavarotti spent seven years in vocal training. Pavarotti's earliest musical influences were his father's records, most of them featuring the popular tenors of the day—[Beniamino Gigli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beniamino_Gigli "Beniamino Gigli"), [Giovanni Martinelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giovanni_Martinelli "Giovanni Martinelli"), [Tito Schipa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tito_Schipa "Tito Schipa"), and [Enrico Caruso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enrico_Caruso "Enrico Caruso").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-tenor-4) Pavarotti's favourite tenor and idol was [Giuseppe Di Stefano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Di_Stefano "Giuseppe Di Stefano").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-tenor-4) He was also deeply influenced by [Mario Lanza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario_Lanza "Mario Lanza"), saying: "In my teens I used to go to Mario Lanza movies and then come home and imitate him in the mirror". At around the age of nine, he began singing with his father in a small local church choir.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-tenor-4)

In addition to music, as a child, Pavarotti enjoyed playing [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football"). When he graduated from the Scuola Magistrale, he was interested in pursuing a career as a professional football [goalkeeper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goalkeeper_(association_football) "Goalkeeper (association football)"), but his mother convinced him to train as a teacher. He subsequently taught in an elementary school for two years but finally decided to pursue a music career. His father, recognising the risk involved, only reluctantly gave his consent. Pavarotti began the serious study of music in 1954 at the age of 19 with [Arrigo Pola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrigo_Pola "Arrigo Pola"), a respected teacher and professional tenor in Modena who offered to teach him without remuneration. According to conductor [Richard Bonynge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bonynge "Richard Bonynge"), Pavarotti never learned to read music.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-6)

In 1955, he experienced his first singing success when he was a member of the Corale Rossini, a [male voice choir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Male_voice_choir "Male voice choir") from Modena that also included his father, which won first prize at the [International Eisteddfod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llangollen_International_Musical_Eisteddfod "Llangollen International Musical Eisteddfod") in [Llangollen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llangollen "Llangollen"), Wales. He later said that this was the most important experience of his life, and that it inspired him to become a professional singer.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-7)

When his teacher, [Arrigo Pola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrigo_Pola "Arrigo Pola"), moved to Japan, Pavarotti became a student of [Ettore Campogalliani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ettore_Campogalliani "Ettore Campogalliani"), who at that time was also teaching Pavarotti's childhood friend, [Mirella Freni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirella_Freni "Mirella Freni"), whose mother worked with Luciano's mother in the cigar factory. Like Pavarotti, Freni went on to become a successful opera singer; they collaborated in various stage performances and recordings together.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-tenor-4)

During his years of musical study, Pavarotti held part-time jobs to sustain himself—first as an elementary school teacher and then as an insurance salesman. The first six years of study resulted in only a few recitals, all in small towns and without pay. When a [nodule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vocal_fold_nodule "Vocal fold nodule") developed on his [vocal cords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vocal_folds "Vocal folds"), causing a _"disastrous"_ concert in [Ferrara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferrara "Ferrara"), he decided to give up singing. Pavarotti attributed his immediate improvement to the psychological release connected with this decision. Whatever the reason, the nodule not only disappeared but, as he related in his autobiography: "Everything I had learned came together with my natural voice to make the sound I had been struggling so hard to achieve".

### Career: 1960s–1970s

Pavarotti began his career as a tenor in smaller regional Italian opera houses. After winning the Achille Peri International Competition, he made his debut as Rodolfo in _[La bohème](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La\_boh%C3%A8me "La bohème")_ at the [Teatro Municipale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teatro_Municipale_di_Reggio "Teatro Municipale di Reggio") in [Reggio Emilia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reggio_Emilia "Reggio Emilia") in April 1961, conducted by [Francesco Molinari-Pradelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_Molinari-Pradelli "Francesco Molinari-Pradelli") and staged by [Mafalda Favero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mafalda_Favero "Mafalda Favero").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-tenor-4) His first known recording of "[Che gelida manina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Che_gelida_manina "Che gelida manina")" was recorded during this performance.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-8)

In December 1961, Pavarotti made his first international appearance in _[La traviata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La\_traviata "La traviata")_ in [Belgrade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgrade "Belgrade"), [Yugoslavia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Federal_Republic_of_Yugoslavia "Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-9)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-10) On 23 February 1963, he debuted at the [Vienna State Opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna_State_Opera "Vienna State Opera") in the same role. In March and April 1963, Pavarotti performed again in Vienna as Rodolfo and as Duca di Mantova in _[Rigoletto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rigoletto "Rigoletto")_. The same year, he performed his first solo non-opera concert outside Italy when he sang in [Dundalk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dundalk "Dundalk"), Ireland, for the St Cecilia's Gramophone Society.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-dundalk-11) He was engaged by the Dublin Grand Opera Society to sing The Duke of Mantua in Verdi's [Rigoletto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rigoletto "Rigoletto") in May and June,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-dundalk-11) and his [Royal Opera House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Royal_Opera "The Royal Opera") debut, where he replaced an indisposed [Giuseppe Di Stefano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Di_Stefano "Giuseppe Di Stefano") as Rodolfo.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-aboutvoice-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-13) In September 1963, he made his debut at Covent Garden in La Boheme, which gave his career a boost.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-14)

In 1964, Pavarotti appeared as Idamante in _[Idomeneo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idomeneo "Idomeneo")_ at [Glyndebourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glyndebourne_Festival_Opera "Glyndebourne Festival Opera")[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-15) and was engaged by the Dublin Grand Opera Society to sing Rodolfo in [Giacomo Puccini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giacomo_Puccini "Giacomo Puccini")'s _[La bohème](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La\_boh%C3%A8me "La bohème")_ and Alfredo in Giuseppe Verdi's _[La Traviata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La\_Traviata "La Traviata")_. Reviewers favourably comment on his singing.

Pavarotti sang with Joan Sutherland when he made his American début with the [Greater Miami Opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida_Grand_Opera "Florida Grand Opera") in February 1965, singing in [Gaetano Donizetti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaetano_Donizetti "Gaetano Donizetti")'s _[Lucia di Lammermoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucia\_di\_Lammermoor "Lucia di Lammermoor")_ on the stage of the [Miami-Dade County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami-Dade_County "Miami-Dade County") Auditorium in Miami. The tenor that was scheduled to perform that night became ill with no understudy. Sutherland recommended Pavarotti as he was acquainted with the role. On 28 April, Pavarotti made his [La Scala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Scala "La Scala") debut in the revival of the [Franco Zeffirelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franco_Zeffirelli "Franco Zeffirelli") production of _La bohème_, with his childhood friend [Mirella Freni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirella_Freni "Mirella Freni") singing Mimi and [Herbert von Karajan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_von_Karajan "Herbert von Karajan") conducting. Karajan had requested the singer's engagement.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-tenor-4)

[Joan Sutherland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_Sutherland "Joan Sutherland") and her conductor husband, [Richard Bonynge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bonynge "Richard Bonynge") sought a tall tenor to take along on their 1965 tour to Australia.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-tenor-4)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-aboutvoice-12) During the Australia tour in summer 1965, Sutherland and Pavarotti sang forty performances over two months. Pavarotti later credited Sutherland for the breathing and diaphragm technique that sustained him through his career.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-tenor-4)

After the extended Australian tour, he returned to La Scala, where he added Tebaldo from _[I Capuleti e i Montecchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I\_Capuleti\_e\_i\_Montecchi "I Capuleti e i Montecchi")_ to his repertoire on 26 March 1966, with [Giacomo Aragall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giacomo_Aragall "Giacomo Aragall") as Romeo.

His first appearance as Tonio in Donizetti's _[La fille du régiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La\_fille\_du\_r%C3%A9giment "La fille du régiment")_ took place at the Royal Opera House, Covent Garden, on 2 June 1966. In this performance, he was the first tenor to deliver nine natural high Cs in the aria "Ah! mes amis".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-tenor-4)

He scored another major triumph in Rome on 20 November 1969 when he sang in _[I Lombardi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I\_Lombardi\_alla\_prima\_crociata "I Lombardi alla prima crociata")_ opposite [Renata Scotto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renata_Scotto "Renata Scotto"). This was recorded on a private label and widely distributed, as were various recordings of his _I Capuleti e i Montecchi_, usually with Aragall. Early commercial recordings included a recital of Donizetti (the aria from _[Don Sebastiano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dom\_S%C3%A9bastien "Dom Sébastien")_ were particularly highly regarded) and [Verdi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Verdi "Giuseppe Verdi")[arias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aria "Aria"), as well as a complete _[L'elisir d'amore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L'elisir\_d'amore "L'elisir d'amore")_ with Sutherland.

His breakthrough in the United States came on 17 February 1972, in a production of _La fille du régiment_ at New York's [Metropolitan Opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Opera "Metropolitan Opera"), in which he hit nine [high Cs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenor_C "Tenor C") in the signature [aria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aria "Aria") and had seventeen curtain calls.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-16) This earned him the nickname "King of the High Cs".[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-17)

Pavarotti sang his international [recital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concert#Recital "Concert") début at [William Jewell College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Jewell_College "William Jewell College") in [Liberty, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberty,_Missouri "Liberty, Missouri"), on 1 February 1973, as part of the college's Fine Arts Program, now known as the Harriman–Jewell Series.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-:0-18) According to his manager at the time, Pavarotti clutched a handkerchief throughout this recital because he had a lingering cold.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-19) Pavarotti himself explained that he needed the handkerchief, since he didn't know what to do with his hands.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-:0-18) The prop became a signature part of his solo performances.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-20) He began to give frequent television performances, starting with his performances as Rodolfo (_La bohème_) in the first [Live from the Met](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_from_the_Met "Live from the Met") telecast in March 1977, which attracted one of the largest audiences ever for a televised opera.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-21) He won [Grammy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award "Grammy Award") awards and [platinum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platinum_disc "Platinum disc") and [gold discs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_disc "Gold disc") for his performances.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In 1976, Pavarotti debuted at the [Salzburg Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salzburg_Festival "Salzburg Festival"), appearing in a solo recital on 31 July, accompanied by pianist Leone Magiera. Pavarotti returned to the festival in 1978 with a recital and as the Italian singer in _[Der Rosenkavalier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Der\_Rosenkavalier "Der Rosenkavalier")_ in 1983 with _[Idomeneo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idomeneo "Idomeneo")_, and both in 1985 and 1988 with solo recitals. In 1979, he was profiled in a cover story in the weekly magazine _[Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time\_(magazine) "Time (magazine)")_.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-22) That same year saw Pavarotti's return to the [Vienna State Opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna_State_Opera "Vienna State Opera") after an absence of fourteen years. With Herbert von Karajan conducting, Pavarotti sang Manrico in _[Il trovatore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Il\_trovatore "Il trovatore")_. In 1978, he appeared in a solo recital on _[Live from Lincoln Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live\_from\_Lincoln\_Center "Live from Lincoln Center")_.

### Career: 1980s–1990s

At the beginning of the 1980s, he set up The Pavarotti International Voice Competition for young singers, performing with the winners in 1982 in excerpts of _La bohème_ and _L'elisir d'amore_. The second competition, in 1986, staged excerpts of _La bohème_ and _Un ballo in maschera_. To celebrate the 25th anniversary of his career, he brought the winners of the competition to Italy for gala performances of _La bohème_ in Modena and [Genoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genoa "Genoa"), and then to China, where they staged performances of _La bohème_ in Beijing ([Peking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peking "Peking")). To conclude the visit, Pavarotti performed the inaugural concert in the [Great Hall of the People](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Hall_of_the_People "Great Hall of the People") before 10,000 people, receiving a [standing ovation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standing_ovation "Standing ovation") for nine high Cs.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-23)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-24) The third competition in 1989 again staged performances of _L'elisir d'amore_ and _Un ballo in maschera_. The winners of the fifth competition accompanied Pavarotti in performances in [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia") in 1997.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In the mid-1980s, Pavarotti returned to two opera houses that had provided him with important breakthroughs, the [Vienna State Opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna_State_Opera "Vienna State Opera") and [La Scala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Scala "La Scala"). Vienna saw Pavarotti as Rodolfo in _La bohème_ with [Carlos Kleiber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Kleiber "Carlos Kleiber") conducting, and again Mirella Freni was Mimi; as Nemorino in _L'elisir d'amore_; as Radames in _Aida_ conducted by Lorin Maazel; as Rodolfo in _Luisa Miller_; and as Gustavo in _Un ballo in maschera_ conducted by Claudio Abbado. In 1996, Pavarotti appeared for the last time at the Staatsoper in _Andrea Chénier_. Throughout the 1980s and 90s, promoters [Tibor Rudas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibor_Rudas "Tibor Rudas") and [Harvey Goldsmith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_Goldsmith "Harvey Goldsmith") booked Pavarotti into increasingly larger venues.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
